name: Key Lime Pie
headnote: Lauren Weisenthal presents this as a deliberately plain, classic version where the short ingredient list means each component has to be good. Her main argument is for freshly squeezed and zested Key limes over bottled juice or concentrate, which is what gives the filling its sharp, clean tartness, and for building the graham crust yourself rather than buying one, since it takes little effort and tastes far better. The salty-sweet crust is meant to cut the richness of the condensed-milk-and-yolk filling, and a mascarpone-enriched whipped cream finishes it. Serious Eats notes the recipe was cross-tested in 2023 and its measurements tightened up.
comment_digest: The most detailed feedback concerns scale: the recipe is built for an 8-inch springform, and cooks using a 9-inch pan found both crust and filling too skimpy. One doubled both for a standard 9-inch plate with good results; another added an extra yolk, four more ounces of condensed milk and nearly three-quarters cup of juice, baked about 25 minutes, and still found the pie somewhat jiggly. That cook's scaled-up crust slumped badly on the blind bake, fixed by freezing the shell 30 minutes, lining it with heavy-duty foil and filling it with pie weights. Regular Persian limes are repeatedly reported to work in place of Key limes. A Florida reader says the traditional version skips baking entirely since the juice sets the yolks. Several readers were confused about whether the mascarpone belongs in the filling or the topping.
flags: 'Load More reviews' present, so only 9 of 15 reviews are in the paste. Two long comments end with 'Read More' and may be cut off. Reader Susan flags an apparent inconsistency in where mascarpone is listed; in this paste it appears under the topping.
